Beállítom A Hold körül keringő NASA-műhold frissen közzétett felvételei szerint egy több mint 180 méter széles krátert hagyott maga után a pályáról letért SpaceX-rakéta egy része, amikor a hónap elején becsapódott a Holdba – írja a CNN a NASA közleménye alapján. A kráterről látványos előtte-utána felvételt tett közzé a NASA: Fotó: NASA Még augusztus 5-én csapódott a Holdba a SpaceX amerikai űrvállalat egyik leselejtezett Falcon 9 rakétájának felső fokozata. A rakétadarab körülbelül 8700 kilométeres óránkénti sebességgel csapódhatott be az Einstein-kráter közelében, a Hold Föld felé néző oldalán. A 13,8 méter hosszú, mintegy négy tonnás rakétafokozatot 2025 januárjában használták egy amerikai–japán küldetés részeként, amelynek célja két holdraszálló egység és tudományos berendezések eljuttatása volt a Holdra. A fokozat ezután maradt az űrben . A Falcon 9 egy újrahasznosítható, kétfokozatú rakéta, amelyet Elon Musk vállalata tervezett és gyártott. A Falcon 9 egyes részei újrahasznosíthatók, és úgy tervezték őket, hogy visszatérjenek a Földre, hogy egy újabb küldetésben alkalmazhassák azokat. A rakéta bizonyos részei azonban leválnak az űrben, és ott maradnak, pályán keringve – egészen addig, amíg végül össze nem ütköznek egy másik égitesttel. A NASA azt írta, hogy hat napba telt, mire a NASA űrszondájának pályája egy vonalba került a becsapódási helyszínnel, majd további időre volt szükség a felvételek feldolgozásához. Az űrügynökség szerint a becsapódási helyszín leképezése rendkívüli pontosságot igényelt. Hozzátették: Bár a rakétaütközés nem volt tervezett, az esemény nem jelentett veszélyt sem a Földön tartózkodókra, sem a Hold felszínére. „Nincs miért aggódnunk. Ez egy technikailag elismert és biztonságos módszer” – mondta Kelsey Young, a NASA holdkutatója. „A Holdat folyamatosan eltalálják különböző tárgyak: meteorok, aszteroidák, üstökösök.” Young szerint a tudósok valójában a becsapódásokat követő megfigyeléseket használják fel arra, hogy többet tudjanak meg a Hold felszínéről. Ivan Noskov, head of the region's capital, Samara, said air defense forces had repelled a "massive" missile attack, with "localized damage" to the city's industrial sites. He also said that medical assistance has been provided to those injured in the attack, but did not give further details. Ukraine has stepped up its long-range aerial attacks on Russian military industries and energy facilities, aiming to cut Moscow's revenue for the war and make Russians feel the consequences of the invasion, now in its fifth year. Zelenskyy says need for peace has to be felt in Russia Writing on social media, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Kyiv's forces had carried out a strike against Samara's Progress Center, which operates under Russian space agency Roscosmos and is involved in producing rocket technology and electronics. Advertisement Advertisement He said that the strike used Ukraine's domestically produced Flamingo missiles to hit the site, which is approximately 900 kilometers (560 miles) from the Ukrainian border. Zelenskyy also said Russia's Savasleyka air base, some 700 kilometers (430 miles) from the front line, had also been hit. "Peace is needed, and this must be evident in Russia — through concrete damage to specific facilities," Zelenskyy wrote. While most of Ukraine's strikes have a range of less than 200 kilometers (125 miles), its longer-range attacks have increased dramatically this year. It launched three times as many of those strikes in July as it did in January, according to data from ACLED, an independent conflict monitor. Repeatedly hitting deep into Russia has forced its military to stretch air defenses over a larger area. Advertisement Advertisement Russia's Ministry of Defense said Saturday that it had shot down 598 Ukrainian drones over 19 Russian regions, as well as the Black and Azov Seas and the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea. Separately, two people, including a nine-year-old child, were wounded when a Ukrainian drone attack hit a private home in the town of Shatura in the Moscow region, local Gov. Andrey Vorobyov said. Child killed in drone strike Elsewhere, a Russian strike on an apartment block in southeastern Ukraine Saturday killed a three-month-old baby and wounded 11 people, local officials said. Drones hit the building in the town of Marhanets, said Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Military Administration. Advertisement Advertisement Meanwhile, hundreds of mourners gathered in Kyiv at a memorial ceremony dedicated to 3-year-old Dmytro Kucher and his grandparents, Halyna and Petro Kucher, who were killed by a Russian drone strike on August 8. Multiple Russian drones destroyed the family's home in the Brovary district, northeast of Kyiv. An initial ceremony was held at Kyiv's Spaskyi Lyceum, where Halyna had served as school principal for more than 20 years, before moving to a churchyard in the suburb of Zazymia, close to the former family home. The couple's son, Oleksandr Kucher, said that his parents had been together since the fifth grade. "They died together," he said. "The Shahed (drone) completely tore my mother apart. We recovered only about two kilograms (about 4.4 pounds) of her remains." Advertisement Advertisement He described his 3-year-old son, Dmytro, as "our little miracle" and "the soul of our family." "He kept my parents, me and our entire family going," Kucher said. Russia's Ministry of Defense also said Saturday that it had targeted warehouses and infrastructure at the Ukrainian ports of Odesa, Izmail and Yuzhnyi. (ALEXANDER NEMENOV/GETTY IMAGES NORTH AMERICA/TNS) By Tribune News Service | Tribune News Service PUBLISHED: September 16, 2026 at 5:54 PM MDT | UPDATED: September 16, 2026 at 5:56 PM MDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... By Ellen Milligan, Bloomberg News WASHINGTON — Last year, a former military officer in the Russian intelligence services named Yuri Khrameev offered $25,000 to a U.S. citizen to track and kill someone in Lithuania’s capital who was “telling lies about Russia,” according to U.S. prosecutors. The allegations were laid out as the Justice Department unsealed charges late Tuesday against five people working for Russia’s intelligence services to conduct attacks and slayings in Europe and the U.S. The defendants remain at large, the U.S. Attorney’s office in the Southern District of New York said. In a series of messages detailed in a U.S. indictment, Khrameev — who was known as Colonel Yuri and allegedly tried to recruit people to kill Russian dissidents — explained that he also wanted to target infrastructure in NATO countries, including train stations, bus depots and warehouses stocking aid for Ukraine. “I am interested in all the countries that are helping Ukraine,” Khrameev messaged the American, after he refused to carry out the killing. “Throw a bottle of gasoline at an electrical substation. Set fire to a warehouse of property or food. You’re looking for such objects yourself. You need to approach it creatively.” “These defendants allegedly operated as part of a global assassination network that reached into the United States, attempting to recruit U.S. citizens and foreigners to carry out killings at the behest of the Kremlin,” said Assistant U.S. Attorney General for National Security John Eisenberg. “Actions like these represent a gross violation of our sovereignty and a threat to our national security.” The federal indictment offers a detailed look at Russia’s expanding campaign of so-called hybrid attacks against European nations that supply weapons and money to Ukraine. The new charges echo a series of cases across Europe this summer. In some instances, Russian security services attempted to recruit citizens or residents in other nations to damage infrastructure or target individuals in return for payment. Earlier this month, Germany officially attributed the recent discovery of an explosive-laden drone at Leipzig-Halle airport to Russia, while Poland said in August that it thwarted an attempted assassination of a U.S. citizen originally from Ukraine ordered by Russia. Estonia also accused Moscow last month of being behind a fire at a defense firm. Two Ukrainian nationals, one recruited online by a Russian-speaking Telegram user, were convicted in the UK of conspiring to commit arson attacks on a car and property linked to then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer. The new U.S. charges illuminate Moscow’s ongoing efforts to murder Russian dissidents and threaten European and U.S. security. This summer, Russian spies also recruited a Venezuelan citizen living in Brooklyn, New York, to surveil and kill a prominent Russian dissident believed to be living in Washington, according to the indictment. Two of them, including one nicknamed ‘Viking’ — a Cuban national living in Russia — told the recruit that they wanted them to make the dissident “disappear” in return for $40,000, which the recruit turned down, exposing their brazenness in wanting to also commit assassinations on U.S. soil. President Donald Trump has adopted a conciliatory approach toward Russian leader Vladimir Putin, as he seeks to reignite peace talks between Russia and Ukraine. ProPublica also reported earlier this week that a Russian oligarch, who has been personally sanctioned by Ukraine over his ties to Putin and accompanied the Russian president on a recent state visit to China, paid for a post-wedding celebration for Donald Trump Jr. earlier this year. The Trump administration has not commented so far on whether it will take action against Russia in light of the new charges. Previous cases — for example the assassination attempt of former Russian intelligence officer Sergei Skripal and his daughter with a nerve-agent in the UK — have triggered U.S. sanctions. ©2026 Bloomberg L.P. Photograph: Gleb Garanich/Reuters Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Explainer Ukraine war briefing: Uncertainty over Kyiv’s Starlink access after Trump claims Musk restored service US president says Starshield military communications system is back, but declines to comment on whether he spoke to Musk on the matter. What we know on day 1,703 Guardian staff and agencies Thu 22 Oct 2026 21.33 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Donald Trump has claimed that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk fully restored Ukraine’s Starlink access , restrictions on which have hampered Ukraine’s attack missions and air defence. However, a senior European official told the Associated Press on Thursday that nothing has changed in the operation of the military-grade Starshield service. The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump had called Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on Ukraine’s use of ⁠the system. Trump on Thursday appeared to confirm that the service had been down, but claimed it was once again working at optimal speeds. “You know, whether I called or whether somebody else called, doesn’t make any difference,” he said. “I guess the bottom line, he put it back.” Questions over who ordered interruptions to Starshield – which plunged relations between Kyiv and Washington to a new low – have ignited a blame game within the Trump administration and its allies . Trump has denied being involved in the decision concerning the slowdown, while US secretary of state Marco Rubio has said that decisions regarding Ukraine’s access to Starlink were up to its parent company SpaceX and Musk, not the White House. Musk last week posted to X: “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.” President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said ⁠on Thursday – before Trump’s latest comments – that Starlink had not ⁠been fully restored. Russia pounded Kyiv with ballistic missiles overnight , after US envoy Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin to discuss the resumption of peace talks. Russia’s aerial attacks hit 12 regions of Ukraine, killing at least four people and wounding scores of others, including five children, Zelenskyy said on social media Thursday. Two women, aged 50 and 60, were killed and dozens of other people were wounded in a Russian strike on a market in Lozova, in Ukraine’s northeeastern Kharkiv region, said Oleh Syniehubov, head of the regional military administration. Another person was killed in other strikes on Kharkiv. Downing Street has rejected the description of Putin as a “humanitarian” made by Witkoff after meeting the Russian president. When asked about the US envoy’s comments, a Downing Street spokesperson said: “We certainly do not recognise that characterisation, and President Putin has killed thousands of people, both innocent Ukrainians and his own Russian people, who he has sent to their deaths on the frontline.” Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha chided Witkoff for flattering Putin, saying on social media the latest “brutal” Russian attacks demonstrate “what Russian ‘humanism’ truly sounds like.” Nato member Denmark said on Thursday it has agreed to buy its first ⁠long-range precision missiles as ⁠it seeks to bolster its security to deter Russian aggression in Europe, drawing condemnation from Moscow. Defence minister Jeppe Bruus said the new missile systems would boost Denmark’s capabilities and enable strikes “behind enemy lines” ⁠if attacked. “We’re in a serious and deteriorating security situation and that ​is why we are ‌building up the defence ‌and strengthening our combat power,” he said. The Russian embassy in ‌Copenhagen said Denmark’s missile policy aimed at confrontation with Moscow and warned of “inevitable disastrous consequences”. Romania will accelerate development of surveillance capabilities and equipment to counter mines ⁠and drones in the Black Sea after a series of drone attacks on commercial ships off ⁠its coast , its ⁠top defence council ​said on Thursday. At least seven cargo ships have been hit near the coasts of Nato members ⁠Romania and Bulgaria in the past two weeks, with 30 sailors reported dead or missing. No ⁠deals should ​be made to buy gas from ⁠Russia as long as Moscow’s war ⁠in Ukraine continues, Finland’s prime ⁠minister Petteri Orpo said in Kyiv on Thursday . The EU banned Russian pipeline gas under short-term contracts ​from 17 June, and will ​apply it to long-term contracts from 1 November next year. Senior Russian political and energy officials meanwhile have urged the EU to reconsider plans to ban imports of ⁠Russian LNG, arguing the bloc’s ⁠low storage levels ​had put Europe in a precarious position. “I ‌hope there is still time to reconsider these decisions,” Leonid Mikhelson, the head of Novatek, Russia’s largest liquefied natural ‌gas producer, told an economic forum in Istanbul on Thursday. “Europe should support its industry, in my view.
